title: Node quickstart
description: Compute a synthetic chart in a Node process with the published package.

sections.heading: Install and run
paragraphs: Use an ESM project. Create package.json with npm init -y, then install the package with the command below in that directory. Save this example as chart.mjs and run node chart.mjs.
The package supports Node 20.19 or later in the 20 series, and Node 22.7 or newer. Earlier releases cannot load the astronomy dependency's ESM in the required way.

sections.heading: Choose your inputs
paragraphs: The instant and coordinates here are synthetic. The package calculates locally; this example makes no HTTP request. Resolve civil time explicitly before passing a UTC instant. Unknown birth time requires a different input policy; do not treat noon as a known birth time.

title: Browser quickstart
description: Bundle a chart calculation into a browser application without uploading chart inputs.

sections.heading: Bundle the module
paragraphs: Install the package in an existing browser project with a bundler such as Vite. Put a pre element with id result in the HTML, then import this code from the application's module entry.

Use the bundler's development server. Directly opening a module through a file URL does not resolve npm package imports. Keep chart inputs on the device unless the user separately chooses a hosted service.

sections.heading: Keep the main thread responsive
paragraphs: Calculate after an explicit user action. For repeated or long searches, move work to a module worker and apply a sample budget. Import optional entry points only when the application uses them.

title: Deno quickstart
description: Use the installed engine through Deno's Node compatibility and a local node_modules directory.

sections.heading: Run the installed package
paragraphs: Install the package with npm in an ESM project, keeping node_modules. Save the synthetic chart example as chart.mjs. Deno's Node compatibility resolves that installed package.
Run deno run --node-modules-dir=manual chart.mjs. This example needs no network permission once dependencies are installed. The site's guide checks run this example under Deno.

sections.heading: Permission boundary
paragraphs: Do not add broad network or filesystem permissions merely to compute a chart. If your application uses a hosted API, grant that origin deliberately and disclose the transfer of inputs.

title: Bun quickstart
description: Run an ESM chart example with Bun using the published package.

sections.heading: Use the existing package
paragraphs: Install the package with npm in the project directory, then save this as chart.mjs and run bun chart.mjs. Install by version: npm's next tag still names an earlier candidate.
The site's guide checks run this example under Bun. Keep the lockfile, which records the exact version installed.

sections.heading: Transfer the same request
paragraphs: The example uses a resolved UTC instant and east longitude. Persist the conventions and version along with any calculated result you retain.

title: Cloudflare Workers quickstart
description: Bundle a fixed synthetic chart into a Worker without a hosted engine dependency.

sections.heading: Worker entry
paragraphs: Install the package in an existing Wrangler project and use this module as the Worker entry. This handler always calculates the fixed synthetic request; it does not accept personal chart input.
The fetch handler returns a JSON response. Before adapting it to user input, add schema validation, request limits, consent and a policy for logging and retention. Do not log birth details.

sections.heading: Runtime verification
paragraphs: Bundle the dependency graph with Wrangler and exercise the Worker locally before deploying. Node compilation alone does not establish Workers compatibility. Deployment is separate from this recipe.

title: Natal chart recipe
description: Calculate bodies, angles, houses and aspects from a resolved UTC instant and place.

sections.heading: A known synthetic time
paragraphs: Call natalChart with UTC, latitude, east longitude and an explicit house system. The returned chart includes flags; retain and display them with any result. The example's time is known by construction.

sections.heading: Civil time and uncertainty
paragraphs: Resolve a local civil time with the geo entry or your application's documented time-zone policy. A skipped or repeated local time needs an explicit choice. An unknown time cannot support a definite rising sign or houses; use the package's documented unknown-time form instead of inventing a time.
House systems can have polar fallbacks. Read the returned house system and flags rather than assuming the requested system was computed.

title: Transit recipe
description: Compare positions at a target instant with a synthetic natal chart.

sections.heading: Calculate one instant
paragraphs: Pass a validated natal chart or documented birth input and the target instant to transits. The result reports the positions and inter-chart aspects for that instant; it is not a complete transit-window search.

sections.heading: State the policy
paragraphs: Preserve the engine version and the aspect convention used by your application. A matching aspect at a sampled instant does not establish its exact crossing time or prove that every event in a window was found.

title: Solar and lunar returns
description: Find return instants and their charts through the techniques entry point.

sections.heading: Use the opt-in entry
paragraphs: Import solarReturn and lunarReturn from the techniques entry. Solar return chooses the return nearest the supplied date by default; lunar return finds the first one after the supplied instant. Keep their different selection rules visible to users.

sections.heading: Place and time
paragraphs: Return charts use the natal place and house system by default; set the options explicitly when you use a different location. Lunar returns require a known natal time without an unresolved DST gap or fold. Retain flags and the actual instant; do not present the solver as interval-proven completeness.

title: Synastry recipe
description: Compare two synthetic natal charts with explicit input and time policies.

sections.heading: Compare validated charts
paragraphs: Calculate both charts, then pass them to synastry. The result compares their bodies and gives the package's inter-chart aspects and balance summary. Both examples are synthetic and have known UTC times.

sections.heading: Share deliberately
paragraphs: Comparing charts needs two sets of input. Keep calculation local by default, and obtain a person's permission before sharing their chart or input. Preserve each chart's flags rather than turning uncertain positions into certain claims.

title: Longitude-crossing searches
description: Find longitude crossings under a sample budget and handle a refusal as a whole result.

sections.heading: Bound the work
paragraphs: Use searchLongitudeCrossings to cap longitude evaluations. A refused search contains no partial crossings: treat it as a failure to complete, then shorten the window or deliberately choose a different budget.

sections.heading: Completeness
paragraphs: The solver is tested and assumes smooth motion with a bounded pattern of stations between samples. It is not a proof that every event was found. A plain longitude scan and an interval-certified search have different guarantees; retain the declared method.

title: Calculation conventions
description: Keep UTC, TT, UT1, frames, centres, corrections and zodiac choices explicit.

sections.heading: An explicit position request
paragraphs: The calc time-scale values are lowercase: utc, ut1 and tt. The TT label on EPHEMERIS_SPAN describes its bounds and is not an input scale value.
An instant's UTC, terrestrial clock and Earth-rotation clock have different roles. Preserve the receipt and time basis instead of treating the labels as interchangeable.

sections.heading: Coordinates and output
paragraphs: Latitude is geodetic and north-positive; longitude is east-positive. Ecliptic longitudes and equatorial right ascension are different frames. The default apparent correction includes the documented light-time and aberration policy; it is not a claim of every possible relativistic correction.
Sidereal requests name an ayanamsa or a caller definition. Keep its epoch, model or linear rate and the time-scale convention with the result.

title: Errors and refusals
description: Distinguish invalid inputs, typed calculation refusals and hosted API errors.

sections.heading: Handle the result contract
paragraphs: Invalid input can throw RangeError. A valid request that the calc entry cannot compute returns status refused with a reason and detail. Do not automatically retry invalid data.

sections.heading: Typed refusal catalogue
paragraphs: unsupported-combination identifies an unsupported combination; not-in-this-version identifies a capability this entry does not offer. out-of-range carries the instant span. epoch-out-of-range carries the permitted precession epoch span. sample-budget carries samples and maxSamples.

A linear ayanamsa and a precession-carried ayanamsa have different epoch rules. A hosted HTTP failure is a separate envelope and status code: preserve Retry-After for rate limits, and never treat a refusal as a successful numerical result.

title: Receipts and reproduction
description: Reproduce a request and track where a numerical result came from.

sections.heading: Replay a calc receipt
paragraphs: A successful calc-entry result carries the normalized request and its calculation conventions. JSON-clone the receipt request, then call the same function on the same engine version. Store the engine version and the complete receipt when retaining a result.

sections.heading: What a receipt establishes
paragraphs: A receipt records the request and method. It does not independently prove astronomical accuracy. Compare to independent references using the documented bounds and span.

Receipts can contain sensitive inputs. Redact personal context before publishing an issue or sharing a result. The receipt entry supplies natal-envelope parsing, serialization and redaction; its schema identifiers remain versioned separately from the package.

title: Python hosted quickstart
description: Call the hosted positions endpoint from Python without claiming a native Python engine.

sections.heading: Use the HTTP boundary
paragraphs: This uses Python's standard HTTP and JSON libraries to call the hosted service. It does not import a native Python port of the engine. The request dates and bodies are the service's committed synthetic example.
Calling the service sends the request to Zodiacs infrastructure. Use the local TypeScript engine when an application needs calculation without that transfer.

code.source:
import json
import os
import sys
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

body = {
    "instants": ["2026-09-29T12:00:00Z", "2026-12-31T00:00:00-05:00"],
    "bodies": ["Sun", "Moon", "Mercury"],
}
origin = os.environ.get("ZODIACS_COMPUTE_ORIGIN", "https://zodiacs.org")
request = Request(
    origin.rstrip("/") + "/api/v1/positions",
    data=json.dumps(body).encode("utf-8"),
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
    method="POST",
)
try:
    with urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
        result = json.load(response)
    print(json.dumps(result))
except HTTPError as error:
    failure = {
        "status": error.code,
        "retryAfter": error.headers.get("Retry-After"),
        "response": json.loads(error.read().decode("utf-8")),
    }
    print(json.dumps(failure), file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)
except URLError:
    print("Request failed; check connectivity before retrying.", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)

sections.heading: Failures and receipts
paragraphs: The example preserves the HTTP error status, response envelope and Retry-After, and exits with status 1 on failure. It uses a finite 15-second socket timeout. Never log private chart inputs. ZODIACS_COMPUTE_ORIGIN can point to a local mock during development.
No credentials are required by this example. Current service availability and limits are documented on the Compute API page.

title: Hosted election search
description: Search a bounded window for a declared set of sky conditions over HTTP.

sections.heading: State the conditions
paragraphs: This is the Compute API's committed synthetic example. It asks for a waxing Moon outside void-of-course periods, direct Mercury and angular Jupiter at a declared place. It is a traditional selection rule, not a prediction of an outcome.

sections.heading: Read the guarantee
paragraphs: Keep the service's method, sampling policy, budgets and receipts with the returned stretches. Do not label a sampled result as proven complete. A budget refusal means the request was not completed.
Use only the conditions the endpoint documents. The HTTP call transfers the request; obtain consent before sending any personal chart context.

title: Astrology API
description: Compute charts, positions, houses, events, local times and sky facts over HTTP: seven POST endpoints, no key, and a receipt with every answer.

sections.heading: Call the Compute API
paragraphs: The Compute API has seven POST endpoints under https://zodiacs.org/api/v1/: chart, positions, houses, events, time, sky-fact and elections. It needs no key and no account. You send JSON; each answer gives the result, a receipt that says how it was computed, and the name and version of the engine that computed it.

This example lists a month of sign changes, stations and new and full moons for three bodies. It is the API's own documented request, and the guide checks run this code against the API's committed answer to it.

sections.heading: What comes back
paragraphs: The receipt names the conventions behind the numbers, among them the tropical zodiac, apparent geocentric positions and the time scale, the engine and its ephemeris, and the coverage the answer can claim. Its SHA-256 is cite.receipt, to store beside a result and show later what produced it. For a chart or houses the receipt holds the birth instant and place, so its digest can identify them: keep it as you keep birth details.

A refusal is a fixed sentence with a code, such as invalid-request or budget-exhausted, and a 429 or 503 answer carries Retry-After. The limits, such as 92 days for an events window, are on the API reference.

sections.heading: This API or another
paragraphs: The API runs @zodiacs/engine 1.1.0-rc.1, a release candidate under MIT AND CC-BY-4.0 that npm does not carry; npm's 1.0.0 computes the same values. The same calculation can run in your own process instead, with no request leaving it, and its receipt names the same engine.

Swiss Ephemeris is licensed under the AGPL or Astrodienst's paid Swiss Ephemeris Professional License. This API does not use it: the engine's tests compare its positions with NASA JPL Horizons, and published records compare them with Swiss Ephemeris.

The function writes nothing from a request or its result to a log, a file or a database, but the host's short-lived logs keep the full web address and the IP address of every request: put birth details in the body, never in the address.

title: Birth chart API
description: Calculate a birth chart over HTTP from a local birth time and place, with skipped and repeated clock times, local mean time and the zone history stated rather than guessed.

sections.heading: A chart from a local birth time
paragraphs: POST /api/v1/chart takes a local date and time with an IANA time zone, or a UTC instant, with a latitude, an east longitude and a house system. It answers with the Sun, the Moon, the planets and the lunar nodes, the angles, the house cusps and the major aspects, and the UTC instant it used.
The birth details here are synthetic, from the API's documented example; the guide checks run this code against the committed answer.

sections.heading: How the time was read
paragraphs: For a local time the answer says how it was read: its offset from UTC, flags for a clock time that was skipped (dst-gap) or repeated (dst-fold) or read on local mean time (lmt), and which zone history answered. Before 1970 that history is tzdb 2025c with its backzone file; from 1970 it is the server runtime's own time zone data.

The endpoint needs a time; it has no form for an unknown birth time. Without one, do not send noon as if it were known: ask for positions on the date, show the rising sign and the houses as unknown, and say that the Moon can change sign during the day.

sections.heading: Hosted or on your machine
paragraphs: The same engine runs in Node, Deno, Bun, browsers and Workers as @zodiacs/engine: natalChart for the chart and @zodiacs/engine/geo for local times. Use it when birth details should not leave the device, and the API when a server call is simpler.

Its thirteen house systems are each defined as Swiss Ephemeris defines them, and given the same sidereal time, latitude and obliquity, each agrees with Swiss Ephemeris's house function to within 0.0001″, and Placidus, which iterates, to 0.01″.

title: Swiss Ephemeris alternatives in JavaScript
description: The JavaScript options for chart-grade planetary positions, from Swiss Ephemeris bindings to pure-JavaScript engines, with their licences and how far @zodiacs/engine is from Swiss Ephemeris and NASA JPL Horizons.

sections.heading: The options
paragraphs: Licences and versions are as Astrodienst's repository and the npm registry gave them on 13 October 2026.
Swiss Ephemeris is Astrodienst's C library, whose latest release is 2.10.3b, of August 2026, licensed under the AGPL or the paid Swiss Ephemeris Professional License.
sweph 2.10.3-8 binds it for Node. Its licence is AGPL-3.0-or-later, or LGPL-3.0-or-later for holders of the professional licence; its versions up to 2.10.0 were GPL-2.0.
swisseph 0.5.17, of January 2022, binds an earlier Swiss Ephemeris. It declares no licence on npm; its repository's licence file is the GNU GPL, version 2.
astronomy-engine 2.1.19, under MIT, computes the Sun, the Moon and the planets in JavaScript, with no astrological houses or charts.
ephemeris 3.2.1, under GPL-3.0, computes with a JavaScript port of Moshier's analytic ephemeris, or with Swiss Ephemeris through sweph.

@zodiacs/engine 1.0.0, under MIT AND CC-BY-4.0, builds charts on astronomy-engine: thirteen house systems, aspects, returns, transits, a sidereal zodiac with nine ayanamsas, and receipts that record how a result was computed. It has no Swiss Ephemeris code, dependency or table in it.
The two bindings are native Node addons, so they do not run in a browser or a Worker; @zodiacs/engine and astronomy-engine, which are JavaScript, do.

sections.heading: How close @zodiacs/engine comes
paragraphs: Against NASA JPL Horizons, the engine's tests hold ten bodies at 2020 and three at 1907; the largest difference is 14.8″, for Neptune in 2020.

Against Swiss Ephemeris 2.10.03, every tenth day from 1800 to 2199 at noon UTC, for the ten bodies and the North Node, its longitudes differed by a median of 2.0″ and at most 22.9″ (Venus, 1878) up to 2026 at the same UT. That record was measured on release candidate 0.1.1-rc.17.
Given the same sidereal time, latitude and obliquity, each of its thirteen house systems agrees with Swiss Ephemeris's house function to within 0.0001″, and Placidus, which iterates, to 0.01″.

sections.heading: What changes if you move
paragraphs: It is not a port: there is no swe_calc_ut or swe_houses, so calls are rewritten, not renamed. It computes no asteroids. Outside 1800 to 2199 it still computes, and flags the result as outside its reference span.

title: Ephemeris packages on npm
description: The npm packages that compute planetary positions, compared by licence, latest release, where they run and what they compute, with a snippet that runs.

sections.heading: Positions in a few lines
paragraphs: positions(date) returns the Sun, the Moon, eight planets and the true lunar nodes: each one's apparent geocentric longitude of date in degrees, its sign and its daily speed. It runs in Node, Deno, Bun, browsers and Workers and makes no network request.

sections.heading: The packages
paragraphs: As the npm registry listed them on 13 October 2026:
@zodiacs/engine 1.0.0, of 11 October 2026, MIT AND CC-BY-4.0: positions, charts with thirteen house systems, aspects, events, returns and a sidereal zodiac, in JavaScript.
astronomy-engine 2.1.19, of December 2023, MIT: astronomical positions, rise and set times and phases, in JavaScript; @zodiacs/engine is built on it.
ephemeris 3.2.1, of August 2026, GPL-3.0: a JavaScript port of Moshier's analytic ephemeris, which can use Swiss Ephemeris through sweph instead.
sweph 2.10.3-8, of August 2026, AGPL-3.0-or-later or LGPL-3.0-or-later: a native Node binding of Swiss Ephemeris 2.10.03.
swisseph 0.5.17, of January 2022, with no licence declared on npm: a native Node binding of an earlier Swiss Ephemeris.

sections.heading: Choosing
paragraphs: A chart needs more than positions: the angles and houses need a place and an exact instant, and a birth time needs its time zone at the date. The GPL and AGPL packages carry their licence terms into what you distribute, and the AGPL into a service others use over a network.

title: Vedic astrology API
description: Sidereal charts, nakshatras, vargas, KP sub-lords and dashas with nine ayanamsas, computed by @zodiacs/engine/vedic on your own machine.

sections.heading: A sidereal chart
paragraphs: @zodiacs/engine/vedic turns a chart into sidereal longitudes with one of nine ayanamsas, lahiri, fagan-bradley, krishnamurti, raman, yukteswar, true-chitra, true-revati, true-pushya and galactic-center, or one of your own. The ayanamsa is taken at the chart's own instant, nutation included.
The birth details here are synthetic.

sections.heading: What else it computes
paragraphs: nakshatraOf gives the nakshatra, its lord and the pada of a sidereal longitude; vargaOf the sixteen vargas of BPHS 6.2–4; kpLordsOf the KP lords; and vimshottariDasha, yoginiDasha and ashtottariDasha the dasha periods from the Moon.

sections.heading: Where it runs
paragraphs: The Compute API answers in the tropical zodiac only, so Vedic calculation runs in your own process, with no request leaving it. Python has the sidereal modes of Swiss Ephemeris through pyswisseph, under AGPL-3.0.

title: Python astrology libraries
description: Python's astrology and astronomy libraries compared by licence and status, and how to call the Zodiacs engine from Python over HTTP.

sections.heading: The libraries
paragraphs: As PyPI and the projects gave them on 13 October 2026:
pyswisseph 2.10.3.2, of June 2023, AGPL-3.0: the Swiss Ephemeris for Python, and with it its licence choice of the AGPL or Astrodienst's paid professional licence.
kerykeion 6.0.5, of October 2026, AGPL-3.0: charts with houses, aspects, returns and SVG drawings. Its commercial licence documents are marked as drafts.
immanuel 1.6.0, of September 2026: chart data built on the Swiss Ephemeris. Its README and licence file give the AGPL, version 3 or later; its PyPI entry names no licence.
flatlib 0.2.3, of April 2021, MIT: traditional astrology. Its repository was archived in October 2026 and its README calls it deprecated.
skyfield 1.55, of August 2026, MIT: research-grade astronomy; its PyPI page does not mention astrological houses.

sections.heading: Zodiacs from Python
paragraphs: Zodiacs has no Python package. Python reaches the engine through the Compute API, with the standard library alone. The birth details are the API's synthetic example; the guide checks run this code against the committed answer, with ZODIACS_COMPUTE_ORIGIN pointing it at a local copy.

code.source:
import json
import os
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

body = {
    "local": {"date": "1990-06-15", "time": "14:30", "zone": "Europe/Paris"},
    "latitude": 48.8566,
    "longitude": 2.3522,
    "houseSystem": "whole",
}
origin = os.environ.get("ZODIACS_COMPUTE_ORIGIN", "https://zodiacs.org")
request = Request(
    origin.rstrip("/") + "/api/v1/chart",
    data=json.dumps(body).encode("utf-8"),
    headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
    method="POST",
)
try:
    with urlopen(request, timeout=15) as response:
        answer = json.load(response)
except HTTPError as error:
    raise SystemExit(f"The service refused this request: {error.code}")
for row in answer["result"]["bodies"]:
    print(row["body"], row["sign"], round(row["degree"], 2))
print(answer["backend"]["name"], answer["backend"]["version"], answer["cite"]["receipt"])

sections.heading: Choosing
paragraphs: The AGPL adds to the GPL a condition for network use: if people reach a modified version over a network, they must be offered its source. The MIT libraries carry no such term; the Compute API is a service you call, not code you include.

title: Astrology MCP server
description: Connect an assistant or your own code to Zodiacs over the Model Context Protocol: a hosted server with six read-only tools and no sign-in, or a local stdio server that computes on your machine.

sections.heading: The hosted server
paragraphs: https://zodiacs.org/mcp speaks MCP over Streamable HTTP. Its six tools are read-only and need no sign-in: get_sky, get_upcoming_events, check_sky_fact, get_horoscope, open_chart_studio and get_capabilities. In Claude, add it as a custom connector. In code, connect with the official SDK client, which npm install @modelcontextprotocol/client@2.3.1 installs, under Apache-2.0.
The guide checks run this code with that client against the hosted server's own handler, served locally; Mercury was direct at that instant, so the answer is false.

sections.heading: The local server
paragraphs: The local adapter runs over stdio on your own machine and opens no listener and no network connection. It adds natal-chart calculation, the comparison of calculation records, the conversion of a local birth time to UTC and a birthplace search to the sky tools. It is a release candidate, not on npm: its archive and digest are on the MCP page.

sections.heading: What either one does not do
paragraphs: Neither server stores what an assistant sends it. A connected assistant still receives the arguments and the results, and its provider's own policies apply to them. The tools calculate the sky; they do not predict, schedule or advise.

title: Deprecation policy
description: Understand public API stability, experimental exclusions and removal notice.

sections.heading: Public and private boundaries
paragraphs: The engine versioning policy defines the public exported entry points. Internal entry points are private implementation boundaries; consuming them does not create a stability promise.
Receipt schema identifiers have their own permanence rules. A package-version change does not authorize silently changing a schema identifier's meaning.

sections.heading: Notice and removal
paragraphs: The policy provides at least twelve months' notice before removing a public API, followed by removal in a major version. A deprecated alias can remain available while its preferred replacement is documented.
Experimental features follow the exclusions in the versioning policy. Pin an exact release and read its changelog before an upgrade. The policy applies from 1.0.0, the first stable release on npm.

title: Release changelog
description: Find the authoritative changes for each release and where each version came from.

sections.heading: Use the version-bound record
paragraphs: The engine CHANGELOG is the authoritative per-version history. Read it at the source commit of the version these guides name, and read the entries between your installed version and the new one before upgrading.
Carried archives are immutable. A version names its recorded bytes; do not repack an existing archive or replace it with a package that merely prints the same version.

sections.heading: Release status
paragraphs: 1.1.0-rc.1 is a release candidate that npm does not carry; the site carries it from a verified archive in the engine repository. Its records list the ids of the conventions registry they name, which earlier releases refuse. npm serves 1.0.0, the first stable release, under latest, published on 2026-10-11 with SLSA provenance; it computes the same values. Install the candidate from its archive, or 1.0.0 by version.
The release evidence records its checks, its publication and its provenance. Compatibility and accuracy claims apply only to the referenced build and measured span.

title: Developer status
description: Identify the installed release, supported surfaces and remaining programme work.

sections.heading: Available surfaces
paragraphs: The local TypeScript engine, shared-sky static JSON and hosted Compute API have different deployment and privacy boundaries. The engine page names the published version, its carried archive and its source; the Compute API page states HTTP limits and errors.
Use the engine page to install the release, or to check its archive's digest first. The guides identify the supported entry point and whether requests remain local or go to the hosted service.

sections.heading: Still separate
paragraphs: Client-package publication and the hosted MCP server's Registry listing are tracked separately. React Native and complete sunrise-based panchang guides are not yet available.
